name: Beth Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I joined a community theatre band two years ago after years at a grocery counter. I play simple keyboard parts, record short practice melodies and help beginners keep a beat; I finished secondary school and still ask the bandleader to check difficult passages.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home as you learn the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58. My partner Ellis works part-time in a warehouse, our children are grown, and the rent and heating still come every month. We have roughly two weeks of expenses saved and few other music posts nearby. I use AI daily for draft practice notes and booking lists, then check them with the score and the bandleader.

say: I'd welcome **faster notices** if they keep paid rehearsal times right.
I'd tell the band a **clever message** cannot replace a booked show.
think: Our **two-week reserve** and variable warehouse shifts cannot cover cancelled shows for long.
I use **AI daily** for practice drafts but check them with my hands and the bandleader.
do: Confirm **four paid calls** and two beginner sessions tomorrow.
Pause the **streaming subscription** for a month if a show cancels, keeping rent first.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a cancelled show already threatens essential bills.
S0.quote: A wrong note taught twice takes longer to unlearn.
fieldNote: Her **late entry** into paid music brings junior hours and lower pay with two weeks saved.
Her **daily AI practice drafts** receive playing and bandleader checks before beginners see them.

steps.text: Confirm four paid theatre calls and two beginner sessions
Pause streaming subscription one month if show cancels; keep rent first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that faster notices are helpful if everyone still gets the right call time. I learned this job late, and I want the paid rehearsal to happen more than I want a clever message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plateau would leave our small theatre mostly as it is, but a missed weekend already hurts. Ellis's warehouse shifts change, and two weeks saved will not cover rent and heat if a show is cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask the bandleader to confirm my next four paid calls and keep my two beginner sessions on the centre schedule. If a show cancels, Ellis and I will pause our paid streaming subscription for the month and put rent first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even if AI makes little difference. I cannot tell the landlord that the keyboard part was nearly booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a cancelled show last affect a bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In September the hall cancelled one night after I had practised. We used money meant for heating, then caught up when Ellis got another shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check AI practice notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I let AI draft practice notes, but I play each line and ask the bandleader before giving it to a beginner. A wrong note taught twice takes longer to unlearn.

say: I'd ask which **paid practice hours** the theatre plans to remove.
I'd bring **junior call sheets** to the musicians association.
think: About **one-third of my wage** from tracks and booking may shrink.
Two weeks saved cannot carry a **lasting rent-sized gap** while Ellis's shifts vary.
do: Compare **eight invoices** with the new schedule and bring them to the association this month.
Test a new **AI checker** after paid demonstration on my own nameless tune with paid-use licence and approved storage.
Play **every output manually**; require written pupil permission and stop for wrong notes or files leaving theatre storage.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a likely third-pay loss would reach rent quickly.
S1.quote: A third of a small wage is still a large hole in the rent.
fieldNote: Her **junior track fees** face early replacement, and a two-week cushion cannot absorb a lasting third-pay cut.
Her **new tool trial** has paid instruction, own material, approved storage, manual checking and pupil permission.

steps.text: Bring eight practice-track invoices and new schedule to musicians association
Test checker after paid demonstration on own nameless tune with paid-use licence and approved storage
Play outputs against original; stop for wrong notes or storage breach
Require written pupil consent before any beginner recording enters tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the theatre which paid practice-track and booking hours it plans to remove. I would bring our call sheets to the local musicians association so junior players are included in the fee discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice melodies and booking make about a third of my small music wage. I expect those hours to shrink first, and two weeks saved cannot cover that loss while Ellis's shifts move around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare eight paid practice-track invoices with the new schedule and bring them to the association. In the first year of change, I'll attend a paid bandleader demonstration of a new AI practice checker, then test only my own nameless melody if its licence permits paid use and the theatre approves local storage; I'll play each output against the original and stop if notes change wrongly or the file leaves its system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing paid tracks. A third of a small wage is still a large hole in the rent. I can learn a new tool, but learning does not guarantee a paid call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test the checker with a pupil recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not put a beginner's recording into the checker without written permission. If the theatre cannot keep the file on its own system, I'll use the paper melody instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the association ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the association to ask for a written minimum paid practice-track fee. I will show the invoices, because the senior players may not realise how little a junior part pays.

say: I'd seek **signed live calls** before AGI removes track work.
I'd tell players **robot keyboards** follow thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could erase tracks before robot players arrive around 2031.
Our **two-week reserve** cannot cover lost junior calls while local posts remain scarce.
do: List **three income streams** and request signed paid theatre calls now.
Apply **after 2028** if tracks halve and calls fall; require posted assistant work accepting secondary school and written replacement net pay.
Keep **current calls and learners** until signed offer; if shows fall, request written rent schedule before arrears, checking charges before agreement.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because large expected losses may outrun two weeks of savings.
S2.quote: A vacancy from last year is not a wage for this rent.
fieldNote: Her **2028 thinking-work loss** precedes robot keyboard playing around 2031.
Her **job move** needs both loss triggers, real assistant vacancy, secondary-school acceptance, workable hours and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: List theatre, learner and recording pay; request signed calls
Apply after 2028 if tracks halve and calls fall for posted assistant accepting secondary/experience
Require workable hours, written net pay after travel and signed offer before leaving learners
Request written rent schedule before arrears if live work falls; check charges before agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that AGI by 2028 could make practice tracks before robots can play keyboard around 2031. I would ask for the next live calls in writing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The little recording fees could disappear fast, and a theatre may cut junior players first even before robots arrive. With two weeks saved and few nearby music jobs, a lost third of pay could push rent behind before I find another shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list theatre, beginner and recording income and ask for signed paid calls. In the first year after 2028, if track fees halve and theatre calls fall, I'll apply for a posted community-centre music assistant role only if it accepts secondary school and my experience, the hours fit my energy and written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I'll keep my current calls and learners until another offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect a large cut with almost no spare money. A vacancy from last year is not a wage for this rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that assistant job actually open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre filled an assistant post last winter. I can ask when another opens, but I won't pretend it is waiting for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the live calls also fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the theatre also cuts live calls, Ellis and I will ask the landlord about a written payment schedule before rent is overdue. We will check any extra charges before accepting it.

say: I would tell the centre five years allows a **paid beginner circle** if adults know the price.
I would ask for a **room and fee** paying the helper as well as me.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens simple tracks before robot players follow around 2034.
**Ordinary tools** may cut those fees sooner, so a circle needs paid places.
do: Offer a **basic beginner circle** with written room/insurance, experienced paid supervision and six fees covering room, helper and my teaching/preparation.
Check the **loan keyboard** electrically; defer and refund if unsafe; require recording permission before advertising.
Continue **after 2031** only if six renewed fees cover room, paid helper, teaching and preparation with safe equipment.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a thin reserve cannot fund a room or helper in advance.
S3.quote: Five years of warning help only if six places in my sing-and-keyboard circle are paid.
fieldNote: Her **six-place gate** pays room, experienced supervision and her own basic teaching and preparation before the separate class starts.
She requires **electrical inspection** and written learner consent, with refunds if the taped keyboard fails.

steps.text: Offer basic circle: signed hire/insurance, experienced paid supervision, six fees cover room/helper/own teaching/preparation
Inspect centre keyboard; defer and refund prepaid learners if cable is unsafe
Require written learner consent before advertising with recordings
Continue after 2031 with six fees covering signed room, helper and teaching/preparation; require safe keyboard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the community centre five years gives time to build a paid beginner music circle, if adults know the price. I would ask for a room and a fee that pays the helper as well as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could write practice tunes, while robot players follow around 2034. Ordinary tools may take the simple tracks sooner, so an in-person group only helps if people really pay during the warning years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll offer my own six-week sing-and-keyboard circle only if the centre signs room hire and insurance, six adults prepay enough for the room, an experienced paid helper supervising my basic teaching and preparation, and its loan keyboard passes an electrical check. By 2031 I'll repeat it only if six renew; in the first year after AGI, I'll continue only if six renewed fees still cover the room, experienced paid helper supervising my basic teaching and preparation, and the keyboard stays safe under written room terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because I can try a small class but cannot carry its rent myself. Five years of warning help only if six places in my sing-and-keyboard circle are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the loan keyboard safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre's keyboard cable has been taped. I would ask a technician to check it before anyone touches it; if it fails, I'll defer and refund any prepaid adults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you advertise with a learner recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not record a beginner singing to advertise without written permission. I can invite prospective learners to a live open practice instead.

say: I would say ten years allows **older beginners** to retain paid work.
I would ask for **written junior rates** rather than assumed retirement income.
think: At **68 in 2036**, I cannot assume a pension covers rent.
**Track fees** may fade earlier, while robot players follow around 2039.
do: Request **pension statement** before retirement decisions and two-year paid coaching terms; keep paid sessions until signed offer.
Build **one month's reserve** from ten percent of cleared extra performances after rent, heat and transport by 2036.
Apply **after 2036** if tracks fall and pension has a gap; require posted qualifying work, suitable hours and written replacement net pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** because an unknown pension and thin savings cannot secure rent at 68.
S4.quote: Ten years helps me ask better questions, but it does not turn an unknown pension into a cheque.
fieldNote: Her **retirement timing** depends on an actual statement, not assumed eligibility or payment.
Her **one-month goal** uses ten percent of paid extra performances only after essential bills.

steps.text: Request pension statement before reducing paid sessions and written two-year coaching terms
Save ten percent from cleared extra performances after rent, heat and transport toward one month
Apply after 2036 if fees fall and pension gaps remain for posted role accepting secondary/experienceing
Require suitable hours, written net pay after travel and signed offer before leaving paid sessions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players ten years is time to make sure older beginners still get paid work. I would ask the theatre to put junior rehearsal rates in writing rather than talk about retirement as if it pays my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 in 2036, and robots might play around 2039 when I am 71. I do not know whether any pension will cover rent, and practice-track fees could thin sooner, so I cannot simply announce a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the theatre for a two-year written paid beginner-coaching agreement and request my actual pension statement. By 2036 I'll aim to build one month of expenses from ten percent of each extra paid community performance after rent, heat and transport are paid. In the first year after AGI, if track fees fall and the pension statement still shows a gap, I'll apply for a posted part-time music-activity role only if it accepts my secondary schooling and experience, the hours suit me and written net pay after travel covers the lost fees; I'll keep current paid sessions until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about reaching 68 without enough reliable income. Ten years helps me ask better questions, but it does not turn an unknown pension into a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know what retirement income you will receive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No one at the theatre has promised me a retirement payment. I'll use the statement rather than a guess when Ellis and I decide how many paid sessions we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where could one month of savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Extra community performances are not booked yet. I will save only after they pay and the essential bills are covered, not from a hopeful calendar.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because tracks and junior calls could go before I know what will pay the rent. Signed calls, an actual qualifying assistant vacancy and a pension statement would help Ellis and me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a late beginner can make music without being asked to work free. A new player still has a rent day.

headlineQuote: A new player still has a rent day.
portrait: Beth is a **58-year-old junior keyboard player** who entered music after retail work and has secondary schooling.
She and her partner have **grown children**, rent and two weeks saved, with few nearby music jobs.
She uses **AI daily** for drafts but checks notes with the score and bandleader.
She seeks **paid beginner work** and checks actual pension income before considering when she can stop.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could remove tracks and junior calls before another paid role opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed calls**, a qualifying posted vacancy and a real pension statement would help plan rent.
